info.name: Minos Tactical Floor Game API
info.description:
Backend for the Indonesian Navy (TNI AL) Tactical Floor Game.

## Response envelope

Every response, success or failure, is the same envelope. A client therefore has
exactly one shape to unwrap and one place to read an error from.

```json
{ "status_code": 200, "message": "Successfull", "data": { }, "metadata": { } }
```

* `data` is `null` on a 5xx, and on a 4xx when the failure is not attributable to a
  named input.
* `metadata` is present only on paginated list endpoints.

**One response in this document is NOT the envelope:**
`GET /assets/unit-class-images` returns a binary zip. A client either saves it or
unzips it, and neither can do anything with a `data` wrapper around a zip. Its 304
is likewise bodyless, as a 304 must be.

## Errors

Every 4xx and 5xx body is `ErrorResponse`. Field-level failures carry a map from
the **request field name** to a human-readable reason, keyed exactly as the client
sent it — so `{"errors": {"name": "This field is required."}}` refers to the `name`
field of the request body, not to any internal name.

| Status | Meaning                                                              |
|--------|----------------------------------------------------------------------|
| 400    | The request parsed but a field failed validation — see `data.errors`. |
| 401    | No token, or a token that is expired or invalid.                      |
| 403    | Authenticated, but not permitted. Also: the account is not Active.     |
| 404    | The resource does not exist, or is soft-deleted.                       |
| 409    | A uniqueness constraint was violated (username, email, hull number).   |
| 422    | The body could not be parsed at all.                                  |
| 429    | Rate limited. `Retry-After` says how long to wait.                     |
| 500    | A defect on our side. The body never contains internal detail.         |

## Authentication

`Authorization: Bearer <access_token>` on everything except `/auth/login` and
`/auth/refresh`.

Refresh tokens are returned **both** as an `HttpOnly` cookie and, when the request
asks for it, in the response body. Browser clients should rely on the cookie;
mobile and desktop clients have no cookie jar and must use the body. See
`TokenPair.refresh_token`.

**Unknown user and wrong password return an identical 401.** Distinguishing
them would turn this endpoint into a username oracle.

403 is returned only *after* the credentials are verified, when the account is

enumeration closed while still giving a disabled user a truthful message
instead of "wrong password". The `System` account can never satisfy either
check: its stored hash is not a valid PHC string, so no password verifies.

request.description:

the request body. Native clients use the body; browsers use the cookie.

Refresh tokens are rotated: the response carries a new one and the presented one
is invalidated. A client that replays an old refresh token is rejected, which is
what makes theft detectable.

item.name: Replace which application roles an account holds

variable.description: The account's surrogate id. Never reused.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on **`/system/roles`** — NOT on `/system/users`.

**That separation is the point of this operation.** Every other route under `/users/{id}`
checks `/system/users`, so an Operator who may correct an account's details cannot promote
anybody — themselves included — to Administrator. Bundling the two would mean one grant
bought both, and "may fix a typo in a name" would silently carry "may hand out
Administrators".

**It is also the only thing that distinguishes the two seeded roles.** As of migration
000025, `Administrator` and `Operator` hold the same 32 permissions; this grant is the one
an Operator does not have. A client rendering the role picker should therefore expect a
`403` for anyone but an Administrator — which is a working boundary, not a bug.

The body is the **complete set**, not a delta, so sending the same set twice is a no-op and
a retry is safe. A revoked grant is recorded as a tombstone rather than erased, so
`user_roles` keeps who removed which role and when, and re-granting the same role later
writes a fresh row rather than rewriting history.

An unknown role id is refused **before anything is written**, so a request naming one bad id
leaves the account's existing roles exactly as they were.

response.name: The account with the roles it now holds.

answered on 2026-09-14: administration is an out-of-game function, so the Casbin

Casbin still cannot answer "may this Operator update *this* account" — policy
objects deliberately carry no instance ids. The question does not arise here,
rather than being answered somewhere else.

Only the fields present are changed; a field that is absent is left alone.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/unit-types`.

Every field is optional; only the fields present are changed. `name` cannot be cleared.

**`id_unit_category` is patchable, so a type can be MOVED between categories.** That is a
real edit — the taxonomy is corrected, not only extended — and it is why the merge happens
against the stored row rather than only against what the request named.

**MOVING A TYPE MOVES EVERYTHING UNDER IT.** The category is reached THROUGH the type, so
every class that belongs to this type — and therefore every hull of those classes — changes
category with it. Existing hulls are NOT re-checked against the ownership rule, so a hull whose
branch does not own the new category keeps existing and keeps working; only its next write is
judged. That is deliberate: the rule governs writes, and the alternative is refusing a taxonomy
correction because of hulls the operator never mentioned, with no way forward except editing
those hulls one at a time.

**`is_system` is not patchable.** It records how a row came to exist; a writable flag would let
a seeded type be relabelled into an ordinary one and then deleted.

item.name: Retire a unit type, and everything beneath it

request.description:
Requires the `retire` action on `/system/unit-types`.

Withdraws the type, every unit class under it, and every hull in those classes — in one
transaction. See `RetirementBlocked` for the one case that refuses this, and `TaxonomyRetirement`
for what comes back.

**THIS REPLACES `DELETE /unit-types/{id}`, AND THAT IS A BEHAVIOUR CHANGE.** The delete was
refused with `409` by the foreign key while any class belonged to the type, so an operator naming
a type that was in use was told no and given no way forward. The retirement cascades instead,
which is what the scope update asked for. A DELETE that withdrew a class's whole hull complement
would also be the most surprising request in the API, which is why the verb changed with it.

**`is_system` DOES NOT BLOCK THIS, and the client must not block it either.** All nineteen
seeded types carry that flag, and it records who AUTHORED a row rather than whether the row may
be withdrawn. A client that disables the affordance on `is_system` rows would make this endpoint
unreachable for every type the fleet actually has. The DELETE this replaces told the frontend
teams the opposite, and that instruction is now withdrawn.

query.description:
Only the types belonging to this category. Resolve the id from `/helpers` under
`unit_categories`. Omit for every type in the system.

request.description:
**The only endpoint that carries the type -> category link.**

`GET /unit-classes` returns each class with its `unit_type`, but that object is the shared
lookup shape, which deliberately carries no parent — so a client holding a class can reach
its **type** and stop there. `unit_types.id_unit_category` exists in the database and is
invisible through `/helpers`, which excludes domain columns so that one column list and one
scan can cover every lookup table.

That made the taxonomy unreachable in one direction: **Kategori could not be resolved from
Tipe or from Kelas by any endpoint.** This one closes the chain, so a breadcrumb
Domain > Kategori > Tipe > Kelas > Aset can be rendered from API data instead of a mapping
hardcoded in the client.

Read-only. Unit types are seeded master data an operator picks from; no route authors them.

## Filtering by category

`?id_unit_category=<id>` returns only the types in that category. Omit it for the whole
taxonomy.

A query parameter rather than a route of its own, for two reasons. These are the same rows
under the same permission, so a second route would need another Casbin object and a new
grant on every role in order to return a subset. And the response shape is unchanged either
way — every entry still carries its `category` — so a client already reading this endpoint
needs no new parsing to use it.

**An id that names no category, and one that holds no types, both return `[]`.** The two
are not distinguished, deliberately: the taxonomy screen draws a row for every category
whether or not it holds anything, and it already has the category list, so an empty result
renders correctly either way rather than being an error to reconcile.

**`?id_unit_category=0` is NOT rejected: it returns the whole taxonomy.** The field is a
plain integer, so zero is indistinguishable from the parameter being absent, and the
`minimum: 1` below is therefore declarative rather than enforced for zero. A client sending
zero sees every type, which reads in the UI as "this category contains everything". Send the
parameter or leave it out; do not send zero.

A NON-NUMERIC value is refused with **422**, not 400.

query.description:
Only the categories this service branch owns. Resolve the id from `/helpers` under
`service_branches`. Omit for the whole taxonomy.

request.description:
The KATEGORI column of the taxonomy screen: every category, with how many types sit
DIRECTLY beneath it.

**THE COUNT IS OF THE LEVEL BELOW, NOT OF EVERYTHING BENEATH.** A category reports its
types, a type its classes (`GET /unit-types`), and a class its hulls
(`UnitClassSummary.hull_count`). That is what lets a drill-down add up: the numbers beside
the rows of one column sum to the header count of the next.

**Why this is not a flag on `/helpers`.** `unit_categories` IS served there — but through
the shared lookup shape, which is deliberately one structure across every lookup table. A
per-table `type_count` would make it eleven shapes and force every consumer to know which
one it was holding. A count describes the TAXONOMY rather than the lookup row, so it
belongs on a route that owns the taxonomy.

**No paging.** Ten-odd rows are drawn in full, and a page of a picker is an incomplete
picker.

## Filtering by service branch

`?id_service_branch=<id>` returns only the categories that branch OWNS. Omit it for every
category.

**Ownership is declared, not derived.** Which categories a branch counts is a mapping the
CMS authors, not a query over the hulls that happen to exist — so a branch shows its
categories even while it holds no hulls of that kind. The taxonomy is a plan, and a plan an
empty warehouse cannot express is not much of one.

**A branch that owns nothing, and an id that names no branch, both return `[]`** — the same
deliberately-unhelpful answer as `?id_unit_category` on `/unit-types`, for the same reason:
the screen draws a row per category and an empty list renders correctly, whereas an error
would have to be reconciled.

**`?id_service_branch=0` is NOT rejected: it returns every category.** The field is a plain
integer, so zero is indistinguishable from the parameter being absent, and the
`minimum: 1` below is therefore declarative rather than enforced for zero. A client sending
zero sees the whole taxonomy, which reads in the UI as "this branch owns everything". Send
the parameter or leave it out; do not send zero.

A NON-NUMERIC value is refused with **422**, not 400.

## Authoring

Since migration 000024 the taxonomy is operator-authorable: `POST` here, plus `PATCH` on
`/unit-categories/{id}`. This paragraph used to read "Read-only. Categories are seeded master
data; no route authors them", which was true when it was written.

**THERE IS NO DELETE ANY MORE — `POST /unit-categories/{id}/retirement` REPLACES IT.** Read that
operation before offering the affordance anywhere. It cascades to every type, class and hull
beneath the category, which makes it the widest single request in the API.

**`is_system` IS NOT A RETIREMENT GUARD, and the client must not treat it as one.** Every
category 000002 seeded carries the flag, and it records who AUTHORED a row rather than whether
the row may be withdrawn. This paragraph used to instruct the opposite — "Disable the delete
affordance on `is_system` rows" — and that instruction is WITHDRAWN: following it now would
make the retirement unreachable for all ten categories the fleet actually has.

**The foreign key stopped being a fallback at the same time.** It used to be what refused a
category holding types, and every seeded category is covered by it. A retirement does not
delete, so the constraint never fires — what limits the damage now is the client's own
confirmation and the counts that come back in the response.

**There IS a soft delete, as of migration 000029.** 000019's argument against a tombstone —
that `is_system` already marks what a migration wrote, so a `deleted_at` beside it would be
"a second, quieter way to hide a row" — is reversed there. The reason it no longer holds is that
the VERB changed, not that the note was wrong: a hard delete cannot express a cascade, because
every foreign key in this hierarchy is `NO ACTION` and a category with types under it could not
be deleted at all. The tombstone is not a preference, it is the only mechanism in the schema
that can carry one.

item.name: Replace a game role's whole permission matrix

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/game-roles`.

**REPLACE, not merge** — the same shape `PUT /users/{id}/roles` uses, and the verb is the
contract rather than a preference. An additive call would let a permission be granted through
this endpoint but never withdrawn, so the matrix could only ever widen. The revocation is the
security-relevant direction: a policy that outlives the row still passes every in-game check.

**`permissions: []` is a valid request and revokes everything.** It says this role may do
nothing, which is what an operator means when a role exists but should not yet be usable.
OMITTING the field is refused with `400`: "I forgot" and "nothing" must not arrive as the
same request, because reading the first as the second silently strips a role's authority.

The matrix is written to `game_role_permissions` — the source of truth, with `created_by` and
a tombstone per revoked row — and the authorization engine is then reconciled to it. A policy
store that cannot be reached is **logged and not reported**: the database is the truth and
reporting a failure would tell an operator their change did not happen when it did. The
reconciliation runs again at startup and repairs any gap.

| `object` outside `/games/` | `400`, naming `permissions.<i>.object` |
| `action` not in the vocabulary above | `400`, naming `permissions.<i>.action` |
| the same pair listed twice | `400`, naming `permissions.<i>` |

item.name: How many hulls each service branch holds

request.description:
The CMS's top-level inventory tabs: one count per service branch.

**THE COUNT IS OF LIVE HULLS**, which is what the drill-down eventually selects. The taxonomy
counts one level down from each of its own rows — a category counts types, a type counts
classes, a class counts hulls (`UnitClassSummary.hull_count`) — and this is the same idea
applied to the axis across the top of the screen.

**Every branch is returned, including one holding nothing**, so a tab with no hulls renders a
zero rather than a missing number.

**Every live hull is counted exactly once.** `units.id_service_branch` is `NOT NULL`, so the
counts sum to the size of the inventory and there is no unassigned residue for a client to
render as "other". A tab for anything beyond these branches has no data behind it.

## Why this sits under `/units`

The numbers describe HULLS, so it is gated on the `read` action for `/system/units`: whoever
may read the register may read how large it is. A `/service-branches` resource of its own
would have needed a new policy object and a grant on every role, in order to serve rows that
`/helpers` already hands out.

A STATIC SEGMENT BESIDE `GET /units/{id}` IS DELIBERATE AND SAFE, and the routers package
pins that routing property in a test — without it `service-branches` would be read as a hull
id and the caller would get a 400 about a malformed path parameter instead of a count.

request.description:
Requires the `create` action on `/system/units`.

**This is not an update.** A new version is appended, the previous one is kept
untouched with `is_current` set false, and games that referenced it continue to see
the numbers the judges actually saw. That is the point of the whole design: a figure
corrected in October must not rewrite a game judged in September.

`version` is **not accepted from the client.** It is assigned by the server as
current + 1. Two operators publishing concurrently would otherwise both choose the
same number, and the difference between "the second is rejected" and "the second
silently overwrites the first" is the difference between a conflict and lost data.
The database's unique index on `(id_unit, version)` rejects the loser, which surfaces
as 409.

Any numeric field may be omitted or sent as `null`, and **null means unknown, not
zero.** The source data carries no submerged speed for any of the four submarines;
treating a missing value as zero would freeze the vessel, and as unbounded would let
it outrun a frigate. A client must decline to compute movement from a value it does
not have, and say so — the generated clients enforce this by making the field a
pointer.

If `turn_rate_max_deg_s` is omitted, the class's `default_turn_rate_max_deg_s` is
used and `turn_rate_is_derived` is set true, marking it as an estimate the CMS can
flag. Supplying a value sets it false, recording that a person asserted it.

item.name: Hand a vessel to a user

request.description:
Closes the vessel's current assignment and opens a new one **in a single transaction**.

The two writes cannot be separated. Between them the vessel has no commander, and if the
second failed it would be left uncommanded with nobody told — which is why there is one
operation here rather than separate "clear" and "set" calls whose order a caller could get
wrong.

Gated on `/system/units` **update**, not on `/system/live-feed`. A commander is a field of a
vessel, in the same way a class picture is a field of a unit class and is gated on
`/system/unit-classes`. The feed object itself is read-only.

An unknown `id_user` is a **400 naming the field**, not a 404: the resource in the path
exists, and it is the body that names a user who does not.

request.description:
Leaves the vessel uncommanded. That is a normal state — a vessel between watches, or one
whose handset is being replaced — and it is what makes the feed honest: a vessel with nobody
aboard reports nothing, which shows up as silence rather than as a stale position nobody is
refreshing.

that the vessel should have no commander, and it already does, so the request is satisfied
either way. Reporting a failure would be reporting that the world already matches.

Gated on `/system/units` **update**, not the `delete` action: this clears a field of a unit
rather than retiring the unit, and keying it on `delete` would let an operator who can
assign a commander not remove one.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/units`.

Every field is optional; only the fields present are changed.

To **remove** a hull number, send an **empty string**, not `null`. An explicit
`null` cannot be used to clear anything: OpenAPI 3.0 cannot distinguish a field
absent from a field explicitly null, so a generated client renders both as a nil
pointer with `omitempty` and sends neither. See the note on PATCH and nullable
fields at the top of this document.

`commissioned_year_from` and `commissioned_year_to` **cannot be cleared at all**
in this version. They are nullable, but the empty-string convention is
unavailable for an integer and `0` is below the permitted minimum, so a year
entered wrongly can be corrected to another year but not back to unknown.
Recorded rather than fixed because the fix changes the wire format and therefore
both generated clients.

Changing `id_unit_class` changes the hull's type, and therefore its category,
because classification lives on the class. Existing specification versions are
**not** re-validated against the new class: they record what was published at the
time, and rewriting them to match a later taxonomy change is exactly what the
append-only design exists to prevent.

**Either field of the branch/class pair may be changed alone, and the ownership rule is
re-checked against the MERGED pair.** Moving a hull to a class its branch does not operate,
or to a branch that does not operate its class, is refused with `400` and
`data.errors.id_service_branch` — the rule `POST /units` applies, evaluated after the merge
rather than against whatever this request happened to name. A check of the request's own
fields would let a single-field PATCH reach a combination the rule forbids.

request.description:
Requires the `create` action on `/system/units`.

`name` is unique among live hulls, case-insensitively, and `hull_number` is unique
among live hulls when present. Both rules are **partial** — they apply only to rows
with `deleted_at IS NULL`, so retiring a hull releases its name for a later
generation. Two live hulls may not share a name; a live hull and a retired one may.

This is what makes the source workbook's duplicate row fail loudly instead of
loading a phantom ship: `KRI Lumba-Lumba` appears twice, both with hull `858`.

## The branch must own the class's category

`id_service_branch` must name a service branch that owns the category `id_unit_class`
belongs to. The chain is fixed by the schema — a class belongs to a type, the type to a
category, and a branch owns categories through an operator-authored mapping — so the two
fields in a create body are not independent.

**Refused with `400` and `data.errors.id_service_branch`**, and the message names the CLASS
rather than the category: the client chose the class and never sees a category, so a message
about one would be unactionable.

The mapping is DECLARED rather than derived from the fleet, so the rule holds for a branch
that currently has no hulls. Today every seeded category belongs to `Navy`, which means a
hull for `Army` or `Air Force` is refused until that branch is given a category of its own
— see `GET /unit-categories?id_service_branch=`.

The hull has **no specification** until one is published — see
`POST /units/{id}/specifications`. An engine cannot move a hull with no known
speed, and the API does not invent one.

request.description:
Requires the `retire` action on `/system/unit-classes`.

Withdraws the class and every live hull in it, in one transaction. See `RetirementBlocked` for
the one case that refuses this, and `TaxonomyRetirement` for what comes back.

**THIS ONE CHANGES BEHAVIOUR RATHER THAN ONLY RENAMING THE VERB.** `DELETE /unit-classes/{id}`
used to REFUSE while live hulls remained, and reported the count inside the prose of the
refusal — the class service's own comment said this was "rather than cascading", because
silently retiring eighteen frigates did not read as a reasonable interpretation of the request.
The scope update reverses that: a cascade under a retired parent is the intent, the client owns
the confirmation, and the same count now comes back as a NUMBER so a client can act on it
instead of parsing English. That also closes the inconsistency recorded as B2.

**A HULL DEPLOYED IN A RUNNING EXERCISE REFUSES THIS** — see `RetirementBlocked`. Planning and
closure are not refused.

request.description:
Requires the `update` action on `/system/unit-classes`. A picture is a FIELD of a
class, so setting one and clearing one are the same capability — see DELETE below.

Send `multipart/form-data` with the picture in a part named **`file`**.

## What is accepted

PNG and JPEG, up to **5 MiB**. The limit is a blast-radius control rather than a
storage one: every client downloads the whole archive, so one oversized picture is
a cost paid by every desktop in the fleet.

The declared `Content-Type` is **not trusted**. The format recorded is the one the
server's decoder identified, because a decoder's answer is a fact and the request's
is a claim. Bytes that are not a readable image are refused whatever the header
said.

Pixel dimensions are checked BEFORE the image is expanded, and it is refused if
either side exceeds 10000 px or the total exceeds 40 megapixels. A few hundred
kilobytes of PNG can declare sixty thousand pixels a side, and decoding that would
exhaust the server's memory — so the bounds are applied to the header, not after a
decode that has already happened.

## Replacing

An upload replaces the previous picture. The new object is written BEFORE the old
one is removed, so a failure at any point leaves the class on a working picture
rather than on none.

item.name: Download every class picture as one archive

request.description:
Requires the `read` action on `/system/unit-classes`. The pictures ARE unit-class
data, so they share its permission rather than having one of their own — a separate
object would let the two drift into "you may edit a class but not its picture",
which reads as a CMS bug rather than as a policy decision.

**This is the one response in the document that is NOT the standard envelope.**
It is a binary zip: a client either saves it or unzips it, and neither can do
anything with a `data` wrapper around a zip.

The archive holds `manifest.json` FIRST — so it can be read from a stream without
buffering the whole archive or seeking to its end — followed by one entry per class
that has a picture.

The `ETag` changes when, and only when, the CONTENT changes. Send it back as
`If-None-Match` and the usual answer is `304 Not Modified`, costing no image bytes
at all. Prefer `GET /assets/unit-class-images/manifest` for the check itself: it
carries the same ETag and weighs a few kilobytes.

Compare the tag, not the clock. HTTP `Date` has one-second resolution, so a
refresh landing in the same second as the previous one would appear unchanged.

item.name: Move a game to another state

request.description:
Authorised by being **this game's Game Master**, not by an application permission.

The route itself carries no permission middleware, so any authenticated caller can REACH it
and only the game's own Game Master is obeyed. That is a widening of who may ask and a
narrowing of who is answered: before participants existed, an administrator was the only
caller who could get here, and any administrator could run any game.

That distinction is the whole reason this is not a `PATCH` on the game. Creating a game is
an application capability — an operator holds `create` on `/system/games` — while running
one is in-game authority, which comes from a participant assignment and is scoped to a
single game. A Casbin object cannot express "the Game Master of THIS game", so the check
is an instance comparison in the service, and a failure is **403, not 404**.

Forward-only, one step at a time:

| From | To | Precondition |
|------|----|--------------|
| `planning` | `preparation` | none — the Game Master decides planning is done |
| `preparation` | `execution` | at least one unit assigned, at least one participant on the exercise side, and every one of them ready |
| `execution` | `closure` | none — the Game Master ends the exercise |

Judges are excluded from the readiness precondition, which is also what makes B5's
"more lenient readiness gate" for Static a statement about a baseline rather than a new
mechanism.

**The gate has three parts, and the last two are the ones that are easy to leave out.** An
exercise that is READY but has no hulls assigned has nothing to manoeuvre, nothing to give an
order to, and no unit for a Commando to lead. And a roster of nothing but Judges satisfies
"everyone is ready" vacuously. The refusal names every missing ingredient at once, under
`data.errors`, rather than the first one found — a freshly created game is missing two of
them, and reporting one per attempt would make the Game Master press Advance twice to learn
two things.

Note also that a **role change clears readiness**, so a game can be refused by a declaration
the caller did not withdraw.

A skipped step, a step backwards, or a step out of a game already in `closure`, is
**409**. Reporting it as a 400 would suggest the request was malformed; it was well-formed
and refused.

hull's commander**. That is an instance comparison over a row — an in-game fact, not an

resource being ordered, but the caller's authority is implied by it: nobody may order a hull
they do not command, and the Game Master who runs the exercise commands no ship in it.

The game must be in `execution`, and must be **accepting actions**. The two are separate
refusals: a game in `planning` has not begun, while a paused one has begun and been stopped.

**AN ORDER IS CLAMPED, NOT REFUSED.** The speed is reduced to the hull's maximum for the
movement domain it is in, and what the caller asked for is returned as `requested_speed_kn`
with `clamped: true`. A client with a slider is not trusted, but an operator whose slider sat
one notch high should lose the excess speed rather than the whole order — the heading is
applied either way.

**A HULL WHOSE SPEED CANNOT BE BOUNDED IS REFUSED**, with 409 rather than an unclamped order.
That happens for a hull in `Air` or `Land` (there is no speed column for either), and for a
hull with no published maximum in the domain it moves in. **In the current fleet this means a
submarine cannot be ordered to move submerged**, because the imported specifications give
submarines a surfaced maximum only — a data gap surfacing as a refusal rather than as an
unbounded boat.

**POSITION AND TIME ARE THE SERVER'S.** The position is derived from the hull's previous leg
and the elapsed assumed time; the instant comes from the scenario clock. Neither is accepted
from the client, which is what stops a Commando placing their ship wherever they liked and
stamping it whenever they liked. A leg is a **straight rhumb line** from that point, on the

query.description:
An instant on the **SCENARIO** clock, RFC 3339. Omitted, it means the scenario `now`,
computed by the server.

changes, so it is routinely hours or days away from real time — a client that sent
`Date.now()` would be asking where the fleet was on a different day. This is also the
closure-playback parameter: pass an instant during the exercise and the answer is where every
hull was then, because each leg is a closed-form function of its own row.

The hull to measure every position FROM. When given, each position also carries
`distance_m`, `bearing_deg` and `relative_bearing_deg`.

**A MEASURE IS A QUERY, NOT A PROPERTY** — the README's §4 — because it depends on where
the question is asked from: the bearing from A to B is not the reciprocal of the bearing from
B to A, and the relative bearing depends on which way the observer happens to be pointing.
This is a parameter on one read rather than an endpoint of its own so that a range can never
contradict the plot it is displayed beside.

The hull must have a **position at this instant**; before the exercise begins none do, so any
value is refused. 400 naming the field rather than 404, because the parameter is not a path
segment and the hull may well be in the game.

**participant of this game**, or hold `read` on `/system/games`. Like `GET /games/{id}`, and for
the same reason — Echo cannot express "this permission OR that participation" as a chain, and a
participant holds no application permission at all. Neither way in gives a **403**.

**A PARTICIPANT SEES THE WHOLE PLOT, INCLUDING THE OTHER SIDE AND THE JUDGES** (decided
2026-09-21). That is deliberately the **opposite** of `GET /games/{id}/units`, which stays
staff-facing so that a Commando does not learn the other side's order of battle — and the two
coexist because **the plot does not exist until the game begins**: positions come from the fix
chain, and the chain is empty until the transition into `execution` materialises an origin for
every placed hull. A participant who reads this during `planning` or `preparation` gets an empty
fleet at any instant they ask about, because no leg exists to answer with.

One state where a participant IS refused: **`closure`**, and for the same reason
`GET /games/{id}` refuses them there — the concept puts closure in the Game Master's and the
judges' hands. A judge-side participant, or the Game Master, still sees it.

**FOG OF WAR IS FUTURE WORK, deliberately not started.** When it arrives it belongs on this
decision rather than in a middleware, because it will be a per-hull visibility rule rather than
a yes/no.

**DERIVED POSITIONS, NOT MEASUREMENTS.** These come from the fix chain — where hulls were
ORDERED to be — and never from `unit_positions_latest`, which holds what a device reported. The
two are deliberately different tables: an order is clamped to the hull's specification and a
measurement is never clamped, so a vessel reporting 35 knots against a 30-knot specification is
the most interesting fact in the exercise rather than a bug to correct. The live feed is where
measured positions are read.

**EACH HULL IS ADVANCED ALONG ITS LEG**, not reported at the coordinates it was ordered from:
a hull two hours into a 12-knot leg is 24 nautical miles further on. A hull with no leg at or
before the instant is **absent** from the list — before the exercise begins that is every hull,
and the list is legitimately empty. The force itself is `GET /games/{id}/units`; this endpoint
deliberately does not enumerate hulls it cannot place, because a client would be tempted to
draw them at (0, 0), which is a real place in the Gulf of Guinea.

**THE THREE MEASURES APPEAR ONLY WHEN `from_unit` IS GIVEN**, and they are computed against the
observer's **live heading** — the heading of the leg in force at the instant asked about — so a
client holding a stale heading cannot get the wrong side of the ship. Bearing is a
**great-circle** bearing, not a rhumb one: §4 records that these are the measure queries, and
"which compass number do I point at" is the great-circle question.

**THE OBSERVER'S OWN ROW GETS A ZERO DISTANCE AND NO BEARING.** An azimuth between coincident
points does not exist, and `atan2(0, 0)` returns 0 — which would report a ship as bearing due
north of itself.

the receipt matrix records **when each recipient read** the message, so this writes a real

request.description:
**ONE ROUTE FOR BOTH OF A7'S DELETIONS, AND THE CALLER DOES NOT SAY WHICH.** The service infers
it, so a client cannot ask for the wrong one and cannot delete a message that is not theirs by
claiming the other verb.

| caller | effect |
|---|---|
| the sender | withdrawn from **every recipient**; still visible to the sender, the Game Master and the Judges, marked with when it went |
| an addressee | hidden from **that recipient alone**; the sender still sees it and is told they deleted it |
| anybody else | **403** — a broadcast is visible to everyone and addressed to nobody, so there is no row to write |

**NOTHING IS EVER HARD-DELETED.** A7 keeps the record for the Game Master and the Judges, and
closure playback must render the visibility as it was **at that instant** — otherwise a Judge
sees a message the personnel provably could not have seen.

way because the sender's act affects other people and is therefore the one they mean; breaking
it the other way would silently make the button do nothing to anybody else.

**IDEMPOTENT, AND THE FIRST INSTANT IS KEPT.** A second deletion succeeds without moving the
timestamp, so the record answers "when did they withdraw it" rather than "when was this
endpoint last called".

request.description:
**SENDING IS A PARTICIPANT'S ACT, NOT A STAFF ONE.** A Commando sends Telegram messages — [6]
has them passing "between Personnels or Actor" — so this asks for a place in the game and the
`send_message` permission, not for the ability to run the exercise.

**THE PHASE IS `execution`.** A message sent in `planning` has no scenario instant to sit on,
and one sent in `closure` would have to be placed on a timeline nobody is advancing.

**`[6.1]` IS ENFORCED, IN BOTH DIRECTIONS.** A Telegram message from the Game Master or a
Judge **must** name `id_assumed_role`: the concept says that staff who want to send one "are
required to 'Act' as some kind of a Commando", so a staff Telegram without one is the Game
Master speaking as themselves into a channel the concept says they do not speak in. The
converse is refused too — a **participant may not assume an identity**, because allowing it
would make the concealment voluntary and anybody could send as anybody.

**`[6.2]` IS ENFORCED IN THE SERVICE.** Administrative messages are "used between Judges and
Game Master", so a participant on the exercise side sending `kind: administrative` is refused
with 403 naming `kind`. It is checked there rather than by a permission because the permission
cannot see the kind, and a permission per kind would put a grant in the matrix that the route
then refuses.

`to` and `cc` makes the message visible to every participant; naming a recipient for a

and an unaddressed one would mean different things to its sender and to everybody else.

item.name: Closure's replay — every action taken, on the scenario clock

query.description:
Earliest scenario instant, inclusive, as RFC 3339 — for example
`2026-09-22T13:00:00+07:00`. Omitted means the exercise's beginning.

This is an **assumed**-clock instant and not a real one, which is why a clock event's own
stored instant never appears here: the window is compared against the derived instant.
Latest scenario instant, inclusive. Omitted means the exercise's end.

Narrows to one stream. **The five ranks are the sort order**, so `transition` events sort
before `clock`, `clock` before `order`, `order` before `message`, and `message` before
`judgement` when they share an instant.

`transition` is a phase move — `planning -> preparation`, `preparation -> execution`,
`execution -> closure` — and it is FIRST because a phase change is a precondition for
everything that follows it. It is also the sharpest case of the rule: the move into
`execution` happens in the same transaction that anchors the clock, so it shares its instant
with the exercise's opening clock event exactly.

**A move appears here only once the game is anchored.** A start declared in Planning anchors
it from the beginning and its early moves land on the scenario origin; a game whose start was
never declared has no scenario instant before Execution, so those moves are absent.

Narrows to the events attributable to one person: **the orders they gave, the messages they
sent, and the judgements about them**. That asymmetry is deliberate — a judgement is written
about a person rather than by one, and the read a debrief is built from wants the marks
against somebody, not the ones they awarded.

Narrows to the **orders for one hull**, and it is the one filter that EXCLUDES the other
streams rather than narrowing them: only an order belongs to a hull. A message is addressed
to people and a judgement is about a person, so neither is returned under this filter.

Continues from where the previous page ended. **Opaque — pass back the `next_cursor` you were
given rather than constructing one.** A cursor carries the whole sort tuple, so a
hand-built one that named only an instant would resume in the middle of a group of events
sharing that instant, which on a paused exercise is every event there is.

Page size. Optional with a default of **100**, which is larger than every other list here
because a client-side playback wants a window in memory rather than a page. Capped at 200.

request.description:
**CONCEPT §4: "Closure is where the 'Game Master' and 'Judges' analyze the 'Game Play'. In this
phase they can view each action taken by each Personnels with playback-like feature (slider or
some sort)."** And §4 answers *who*: *"The closure phase is only accessible by the 'Game Master'
and 'Judges'"*. So a caller must hold `read` on `/games/timeline` **and** be a participant of this
exercise.

**A MERGE OF FOUR STREAMS IN ONE SEQUENCE ON THE SCENARIO CLOCK.** Orders, messages, judgements
and changes to the clock itself, ordered by `assumed_at` and then by a **pinned tiebreak**:
events share an instant routinely — several orders arrive in one tick, and **during a pause the
clock does not move at all, so every action taken while paused carries the identical instant** —
so the sort is on `(assumed_at, type rank, id)` and all three are part of the cursor. Two
identical requests cannot return one instant's events in two different orders.

**NOTHING IS MASKED AND NOTHING IS FILTERED, AND THAT IS THE PHASE RATHER THAN AN OVERSIGHT.**
A8 makes withdrawn messages visible to the Game Master and the Judges, and F5 reveals identities
at Closure. So a withdrawn message IS returned, carrying `sender_deleted_at` **and** each
recipient's `deleted_at`; and a message sent under an assumed identity carries the assumed role
**and** the real author, because the concealment is part of what is being analysed rather than
something to be tidied away.

**A CLOCK EVENT'S `assumed_at` IS COMPUTED, AND THE RESULT IS WORTH KNOWING.** The stored instant
is on the REAL clock, so the scenario instant is derived from it. Two consequences a client will
see: the opening event lands exactly on the instant the exercise's scenario clock started, and a
pause and the resume that followed it can share one `assumed_at` — because from the scenario's
point of view no time passed between them.

**THE SEQUENCE IS STABLE, AND A CLIENT MAY RELY ON IT.** Closure is terminal: no orders arrive,
no messages are sent, no judgements are recorded. So a page taken now is the same page taken
later, and the whole replay can be held for the life of the phase. That is what makes the
analysis meaningful, and it is a property of the lifecycle rather than a promise this endpoint
invents.

request.description:
The room key is the ONLY input: the client does not know the game id yet, which is exactly
what this call is for. It answers with the game AND the caller's own participant row, so a
freshly installed app learns in one request what it has entered, what it may do there, and
whether it has already declared readiness.

**Authentication only.** What authorises the call is holding a place in the game the key
belongs to — an instance fact, which a Casbin object cannot express because objects name
resource families and carry no instance id.

**A wrong key is 404** — the same 404 a discarded game produces, so the endpoint cannot be
used to tell a key that never existed from one whose exercise was cancelled.

**A valid key held by a non-participant is 403.** Not 404: they hold a real key, so the room
plainly exists, and telling them otherwise would send them hunting for a typo in a key that
is correct. The remedy is to ask the Game Master for a place, and only a 403 says that. It
leaks nothing — a guessed key is never the valid one, so somebody guessing only ever sees
the 404.

**Refused at `closure`** for a participant the rules eject from it, on the same terms as
`GET /games/{id}`. Both refusals exist because one is not enough: a participant who cannot
READ a game must not be able to enter it through the other door either.

The key is stored unhashed, unlike every other secret in this API, because it is
TRANSCRIBED — read aloud or copied off a board and typed into a handset — and a hash cannot
be read out. Migration 000017 records that as a decision rather than an oversight.

request.description:
Accepts up to 60 fixes from one vessel's beacon. This is the endpoint the mobile app calls.

**Authorised by being this vessel's current commander — not by a permission.** A Casbin
object names a resource family and carries no instance id, so "may this user report for
THIS ship" is not expressible as a policy. The check is an instance comparison in the
service, and the same reasoning applies to `GET /live-feed/me`.

A refusal is **403, not 404**: the vessel exists and the caller may have listed it a moment
earlier, so reporting a blocked report as "not found" would hide it from the audit trail.
Only a vessel that genuinely does not exist is a 404.

## What the server does with `recorded_at`

The client sends when it *believes* it observed each fix; the server decides whether that
is a live report or a backlog.

| Gap from the server's clock | Treatment |
|---|---|
| within ±60 s | **live** — `recorded_at` is re-stamped with the server's time |
| older than 60 s, within 30 days | **backfill** — the device's `recorded_at` is kept |
| older than 30 days | **refused**, counted in `rejected` |

Re-stamping a live fix is not tidiness. A `recorded_at` in the future would become the
vessel's latest position, and the guard that discards out-of-order fixes would then discard
every honest fix until real time caught up — a ship reporting steadily that never moves on
the map. A device clock more than a minute ahead is therefore treated as live, re-stamped,
and logged as a warning.

Keeping a backfill's own timestamp is the mirror of the same argument: a backlog's whole
value is *where the vessel was when it could not report*, and re-stamping it to now would
draw a straight line the ship never sailed.

## Rejections

Age is the only per-fix refusal, and it is permanent — an out-of-retention fix cannot be
made valid by sending it again. The response therefore carries **counts**, not a list of
complaints with nothing to act on. A batch in which every fix was refused is still a
**200**: the request was understood and each fix was examined, and the counts are the
answer.

## Ordering

Fixes may arrive in any order, and the vessel's latest position is taken from the **newest
fix in the batch by `recorded_at`** — not the last one sent. A backlog flushed after a
reconnect interleaves old points among new ones, so the last one sent is frequently not the
newest one observed.

How the batch was handled. Every response to a well-formed batch is 200, including one
in which nothing was accepted.

request.description:
Requires `create` on `/system/hierarchy`.

**THE INTERESTING CASE IS INSERTING IN THE MIDDLE.** A future Koarmada belongs between Gugus
and Operasi Gabungan, and a level below Unsur is the same problem at the other end, so the
request says WHERE the new level goes rather than what number it gets. The server renumbers.

`insert_after_id` names the level the new one ranks **directly above**, so one field covers
all three positions:

| `insert_after_id` | result |
|---|---|
| omitted | the new level becomes the LOWEST, below everything |
| any id | the new level sits immediately above that level |
| the highest level's id | the new level becomes the HIGHEST, above everything |

"After" reads against this list as a client displays it — lowest first — so the new level
appears immediately after the named one. Sending a raw `echelon_rank` instead would put the
dense numbering and the renumbering it needs in the caller's hands.

**400 if `insert_after_id` names a level that does not exist.** There is deliberately no
fallback to the top or the bottom: a client holding a stale list would otherwise renumber
every level in the system while the operator watched for a reason they could not see.

**409 if the name is already in use.** Names are unique across the vocabulary.

**THE NEW LEVEL IS NEVER A SYSTEM ROW**, so the CMS may offer to remove it. The four seeded
levels carry `is_system`, which stops the default hierarchy being deleted and leaving a
system whose vocabulary is a blank page.
